jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for Question 3, stating the question to be treated—whether an angel is in place—and cross-referencing the parallel treatment in Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.52, a.1.
concepts: cross-reference to Aquinas ST I q.52 a.1

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e115.summary: First objection against an angel being in place: if it belonged to an angel to be in place, this would be by reason of essence, power, or operation. Not by essence, since (per Avicenna) place does not belong even to corporeal things by reason of substance, still less to spiritual things like angels. Not by power, since an angel's power is either identical with its essence or, if not, is equally abstracted from quantity and place as essence is. Not by operation either, since an angel could operate on nothing regarding place and would then be nowhere—and even when an angel does act on the heavenly body (its chief object of operation), that body itself is not in place, per Physics IV (earth in water, water in air, air in fire, fire in heaven, but heaven in nothing further).
claims: Being in place, if it belonged to an angel, would have to be by reason of essence, power, or operation
Place does not belong to substance even in corporeal things, so still less to spiritual essence or an angel's power (abstracted from quantity like its essence)
The heavenly body, the chief object of angelic operation, is not itself in place, so operation cannot ground an angel's being in place either
Therefore an angel is not in place
concepts: essence, power, and operation as possible grounds of presence in place
the heavens as not themselves in place

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e157.summary: Second objection: per Boethius (De Hebdomadibus), it is a common conception that incorporeal things are not in place; angels are posited as incorporeal; therefore angels are not in place.
claims: It is a common conception (per Boethius) that incorporeal things are not in place
Angels are incorporeal
Therefore angels are not in place

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e169.summary: Sed contra: John Damascene (De Fide Orthodoxa I.16) states that an incorporeal nature is where it operates; an angel operates in place; therefore an angel is in place.
claims: Damascene holds that an incorporeal nature is where it operates
An angel operates in place
Therefore an angel is in place
concepts: Damascene on incorporeal presence via operation

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e180.summary: Opens the responsio by announcing a two-part procedure: first, what is clear about the question will be established; second, what is doubtful will be investigated.
concepts: division of the response into settled and disputed matters

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e191.summary: Establishes the clear preliminary distinctions. Following Damascene and Physics IV, place is the corporeal boundary of a container with respect to what it contains; strictly speaking, only what is so contained as to be terminated by place as an extrinsic boundary and commensurate with it is 'in place'—this is being circumscribed by place, and no one but those who held angels corporeal ever placed angels in place this way. More broadly, 'being in place' can mean being determinately present to this or that place and distant from a remote one without being circumscribed by any—called by some 'being in situ.' This broad sense divides further into mathematical and natural place, according to the quantitative and qualitative natures considered in place; by the natural mode, a thing is determinately in its natural place when its nature inclines it there such that it is in it by nature and out of it only by violence—and in this sense too no one says an angel is in place, since by nature an angel does not depend on one place more than another the way a conserved thing depends on its conserver.
claims: Strict circumscriptive presence in place, proper to bodies, has never been attributed to angels except by those who held them corporeal
A broader sense of 'being in place'—determinate presence without circumscription, called 'being in situ'—divides into mathematical and natural place

In the natural sense, being in place requires a natural inclination toward that place as by connaturality (as conserved to conserver); angels lack such inclination and so are not in natural place in this sense either

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e256.summary: Notes an opinion approaching this natural-place sense, holding that angels are by nature assigned to move determinate heavenly bodies and so cannot immediately move anything else or be elsewhere—an opinion judged erroneous and irrational, since a spiritual creature's external action proceeds from free will, not natural necessity, and so cannot by nature be necessarily determined to one thing such that it could not do otherwise (whatever divine ordination might add). It then explains 'place' taken metaphysically as belonging to whatever bears such a relation to place that it is neither everywhere nor nowhere but somewhere—though not by nature more here than there—so that while here it is not elsewhere but distant according to locational distance; a mathematical body, lacking self-determination to any one place, would still necessarily be in some place, though not circumscriptively (since it would be quantified) while an angel, not being quantified, cannot be determined to place circumscriptively. Setting circumscription aside, the remaining question is whether an angel is in some place in this indeterminate-but-necessary sense.
claims: The view that angels are by nature fixed to moving specific heavenly bodies is erroneous, since spiritual creatures act by free will, not natural necessity
Metaphysically, 'place' belongs to whatever is neither everywhere nor nowhere but somewhere, without natural determination to one place over another
The remaining question is whether an angel is necessarily in some (non-circumscribed) place in this sense
concepts: free will versus natural necessity in spiritual creatures

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e311.summary: Introduces four opinions on the question, beginning with the first: that an angel, in the sense just described, determines itself to a place in which it is definitively, the ground of this definitive presence being its own essence, insofar as that essence is finite and limited. This opinion is supported by three reasons.
claims: Opinion 1: an angel is in a place definitively, and the reason for this is the finitude/limitation of its own essence
concepts: finitude of essence as ground of place

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e327.summary: First reason for Opinion 1: drawn from comparing the angel's essence to the divine essence under the aspect of finite and infinite. As an infinite substance is such as to be everywhere, so a finite essence is such as to be somewhere and not everywhere; God, on account of the infinity of his essence, is everywhere; therefore an angel, on account of the finitude and limitation of its essence, is determinately somewhere.
claims: Infinite essence grounds being everywhere; finite essence grounds being determinately somewhere
Since God is everywhere by infinite essence, an angel, having finite essence, is determinately somewhere
concepts: analogy between divine ubiquity and angelic location

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e348.summary: Second reason for Opinion 1: drawn from angelic operation. By nature, an active cause is present to its passive object prior to acting on it (as fire is naturally present to the combustible before burning it), and this holds generally for all active and passive things—proximity must precede action. Since an angel acts on a determinate place or body existing in a determinate place, and not everywhere simultaneously, the angel by its nature is present to a place before acting there; hence the angel's operation on place is not itself the reason for its being in place (since it is already there before acting), but rather the angel's very essence, by which it is present to place, precedes its acting there.
claims: An active cause must be naturally present to its passive object before acting on it
Since an angel is present to a determinate place before acting on it, its operation cannot be the reason for its presence in place
Therefore the angel's essence itself, not its operation, is the reason for its presence in place
concepts: essence as ground of presence versus operation

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e377.summary: Third reason for Opinion 1: drawn from the angel's relation to the universe of which it is a part. A part is not outside its whole; an angel is a part of the universe; therefore it is not outside the universe but within it—yet not everywhere within it, since then it would be equal to the whole; therefore it is determinately somewhere.
claims: A part cannot be outside the whole to which it belongs
An angel is a part of the universe, hence within it
Being everywhere within the universe would make the angel equal to the whole, which is impossible; hence the angel is determinately somewhere
concepts: angel as part of the universe

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e390.summary: Cites supporting authorities for Opinion 1: Damascene (II.2), who says spirits are contained by walls, doors, bars, and seals, and the episcopal article condemning the claim that an angel or separated soul is nowhere—arguing that if essence were not the angel's reason for being in place, it would sometimes be nowhere at all, since an angel sometimes operates on nothing regarding place; since essence alone seems available to ground its presence in such cases, essence must be that reason.
claims: Damascene states that spirits are contained by physical barriers
A condemned article holds it erroneous to say an angel or separated soul is nowhere
Since an angel sometimes has no operation on place, only its essence can account for its always being somewhere
concepts: Damascene on spirits and physical containment
essence as necessary ground when operation is absent

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e412.summary: Rejects Opinion 1, appealing to another article which clarifies that the proposition 'an angel is nowhere according to substance' is erroneous only if taken to mean substance is not in place at all; but it is true if taken to mean that substance is not the reason for being in place—indeed that same article expressly states the angel's essence is not for it the reason for being in place. This will now be proved along the same three lines used to support Opinion 1: the limitation of the angel's essence, its operation, and its status as a part of the universe.
claims: The condemned proposition is erroneous only under the reading that substance is not in place at all, not under the reading that substance is not the reason for being in place
It is true, and will be argued, that the angel's essence is not the reason for its being in place
The refutation proceeds via the same three approaches used to argue for Opinion 1
concepts: essence as not the ground of place

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e434.summary: First refutation (via limitation of essence): distinguishes two kinds of limitation—limitation according to quiddity/essence, whereby every creature is bounded by definite limits (hence definition, which states what a thing is, is called a 'boundary' in Metaphysics V), and limitation according to quantity of mass, whereby a creature is of a certain size and no larger, which alone necessarily entails a relation to situs such that the thing must be somewhere, not everywhere or nowhere, and while here is not elsewhere. An angel lacks the second kind of limitation (not being quantified by mass), so cannot on that basis be in place. Nor does the first kind ground place: if essential limitation corresponded to definitive place as quantitative limitation corresponds to circumscriptive place, then—just as a finite quantum can only be circumscribed by an equal place—a finite essence could only be defined by a place proportioned to it, which is absurd, since no place is equal or unequal to an angel's essence, these being of wholly different orders, and no author holds such a proportion. By the same reasoning, God is not everywhere by reason of the infinity of his substance either, but only by reason of his effects (as established in the preceding question); for if infinite essence necessarily entailed being 'wherever,' it would entail necessarily being in an infinite place, whereas being everywhere is not the same as being in an infinite place, so the infinity of the divine essence is not itself the reason for God's being everywhere, contrary to what the first reason of the other opinion assumed.
claims: Essential (quidditative) limitation, unlike quantitative-mass limitation, does not entail a necessary relation to place

If essential limitation grounded definitive place as quantitative limitation grounds circumscriptive place, it would absurdly require a place exactly proportioned to the angel's essence, which no place is
By parallel reasoning, God's infinite essence is not itself the reason for his being everywhere (only his effects are, per the prior question), refuting the first reason for Opinion 1
concepts: critique of the finite/infinite-essence analogy applied to place

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e525.summary: States a counter-objection to the preceding refutation: one might say the corporeal case (quantum to circumscribing place), the angelic case (angel to defining place), and the divine case (God to infinite place) are not parallel, because God and angel are free substances—so by reason of its freedom an angel can be in a greater or lesser (though finite) place, and God can be in an infinite place (if one existed) or a finite one, since the finite is contained within the infinite—whereas a corporeal quantum, lacking such freedom, is necessarily confined to a place exactly equal to it.
claims: It might be objected that freedom distinguishes God and angels from bodies, allowing them variable location in a way bodies cannot have
concepts: freedom as a disanalogy between spiritual and corporeal presence in place

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e550.summary: Rejects the freedom-based objection: although God and angel are free substances, this freedom pertains only to what is subject to their operation, not to what belongs to them independently of and prior to all operation; but whatever belongs to God or angel by reason of the finitude or infinity of their substance belongs to them independently of all operation, since that finitude or infinity is prior to any operation of the substance—hence there is no freedom in God or angel regarding being in a greater or lesser, finite or infinite, place, if finitude or infinity of essence is what grounds being in place at all. Illustrated by the case of a man, a free but quantified corporeal being: just as it is not in his power to be of greater or lesser bodily size, so it is not in his power to be in a greater or lesser place, but he is necessarily in an equal one; likewise, though God and angel are free with respect to the external things to which they are compared through their operations, it is no more in their power to be of greater or lesser essential perfection than it is in their power to be in a greater place, if quantity of essential perfection is what grounds being in place.
claims: Freedom pertains only to what is subject to operation, not to what precedes all operation, such as finitude or infinity of essence
Therefore freedom cannot explain variable location if essential finitude/infinity is what grounds being in place
The human case illustrates the point: bodily size (and correspondingly, required place) is not subject to the will, even though the person is otherwise free
concepts: scope of freedom versus what precedes operation
essential perfection and its non-relation to variable location

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e598.summary: Second refutation (via operation), answering the second reason for Opinion 1: being immediately present to something extends more broadly than being locally proximate to it. This is shown because the inference does not convert: it follows that what is locally immediately proximate to something is immediately present to it, but not conversely, that what is immediately present to something is locally proximate to it—for instance, the soul is immediately present to the body, and form universally to matter, yet these are not locally near or far, since the presence of form to matter (or accident to subject) is of a different kind than local presence and does not include it; had God created an angel composed of matter and form before the corporeal world, its form would have been immediately present to its matter without any spatial proximity. Since one cannot validly infer the less common (local proximity) from the more common (immediate presence)—doing so is the fallacy of the consequent—and since being immediately present to something is broader than being locally proximate to it, one cannot infer from an angel's immediate presence to a place that it must be locally proximate to it before acting; it suffices that the active be immediately present to the passive prior to acting by order of nature, not that it be locally proximate—it suffices to be present by order rather than by situs, as will be further explained. This resolves the second reason for the other opinion.
claims: Immediate presence is broader than local proximity: the inference from immediate presence to local proximity is invalid (fallacy of the consequent)
Form is immediately present to matter without being locally near or far, illustrating presence without spatial proximity
Therefore an angel's presence to a place, required prior to acting on it, need not be local/spatial proximity but presence by 'order,' refuting Opinion 1's second reason

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e681.summary: Third refutation (via being a part of the universe): distinguishes two senses of 'universe'—the totality of bodies and corporeal perfections alone, or the totality of all things, corporeal and spiritual. Under the first sense, every body and corporeal perfection bears a relation to place with the differentiae 'within' and 'without,' so every part of this corporeal universe must be within it; but an angel is not a part of this corporeal universe, so it need not be within it according to any situs or place—here Opinion 1's third reason errs, having proceeded as though the angel were a part of the corporeal universe. Under the second sense, the angel is indeed a part of the universe of all things, but from this one cannot argue it is in some place definitively—rather the opposite, since it would be improper for the differentiae proper to one part (the corporeal universe)—within/without, near/far, above/below, here/there, grounded in quantity, to which situs belongs per se—to extend to all parts of the universe taken absolutely, of which the corporeal universe is only a part; these differentiae therefore do not extend to incorporeal substances such as angels. This is contradicted only by an imagination that cannot transcend quantity and the continuous, picturing angels as extremely subtle quanta—but imagination should not be trusted here, since angels really abstract from quantity as from quality: as they are not white or black, hot or cold, so they are not great or small, not being quantified, and hence not 'here' or 'there' by reason of their essence, these being properties of the quantified alone. Nor does Damascene's earlier-cited text tell against this: some manuscripts prefix a negation ('they are not contained'), and even granting no such negation, Damascene himself glosses the passage—'intellects existing in intelligible places'—to mean that angels are intelligibly in place because they are understood to be where they operate; and the condemned article does not tell against this either, since it is explained by the other article as noted.
claims: Under the sense of 'universe' as the corporeal totality, an angel, not being a corporeal part, need not be located within it—Opinion 1's third reason errs by treating the angel as a corporeal part

Under the sense of 'universe' as the totality of all things, the angel is a part but this does not entail definitive location, since the spatial differentiae proper to corporeal parts cannot properly extend to incorporeal parts

Imagination, which cannot transcend quantity, wrongly pictures angels as subtle quanta; angels truly abstract from quantity as from quality and so are neither great nor small, here nor there, by their essence
Damascene's text, properly read (with or without the textual negation), means angels are intelligibly 'in place' because understood to be where they operate, not that they are spatially contained
concepts: corporeal universe versus universe of all things
critique of imagination as a guide to incorporeal reality

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e766.summary: States Opinion 2: an angel is not in place such that its essence is the reason for being in place, but rather its operation on place, or on a body existing in place, is the reason—yet in such a way that it is the angel's very essence (not merely its operation) to which being in place belongs, such that while the angel is in one place it is not in another, but is distant from a distant place and near to a near one; thus situs and its properties belong to the angel's essence itself, without circumscription.
claims: Opinion 2: the angel's operation (on place or a body in place) is the reason it is in place, but the resulting presence, once grounded, belongs to the angel's essence itself, without circumscription
concepts: operation as ground of essential (non-circumscribed) presence

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e786.summary: A methodological remark: the author will proceed inquisitively regarding this and the following opinions, asserting nothing definitively. A possible difficulty is raised: when it is said that an angel's operation is the reason for its being in place, this cannot mean immanent operation (understanding and willing), since such operation is as abstracted from situs as the angel's essence itself; it must instead mean operation transeunt into external matter.
claims: The following discussion of opinions 2-4 is offered inquisitively, without assertion
'Operation' as the reason for an angel's being in place must mean transeunt operation on external matter, not immanent acts of intellect and will

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e808.summary: Argues that transeunt operation cannot be the reason an angel is in place definitively: as quantity relates to body as the reason for its being in place circumscriptively, so operation relates to angel as the (proposed) reason for its being in place definitively; but quantity, considered as a subject distinct from the body, cannot be the body's reason for being in place circumscriptively (the major premise, granted on the other opinion's own terms); therefore operation, as a subject distinct from the angel—being that which passes into remote external matter—cannot be the angel's reason for being in place definitively (the minor being self-evident).
claims: By analogy with quantity's relation to a body's circumscriptive presence, a transeunt operation distinct from the angel cannot ground the angel's definitive presence in place
concepts: subject-distinct accident as inadequate ground of presence

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e833.summary: A further argument: a body's being quantified does not prevent it from also relating to another body as mover to moved. So if a transeunt operation directed toward something else were the reason for a thing's being definitively in place, it would follow that a moving body is simultaneously in two places—one circumscriptively, by its own quantity, and another definitively, by its motion or operation passing into the other body—which seems altogether absurd.
claims: If transeunt operation grounded definitive presence in place, a moving body would absurdly be simultaneously in two places—one circumscriptive, one definitive

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e853.summary: States Opinion 3: an angel is in place neither by essence, nor by operation, nor by anything else, such that place, situs, or the differentiae/properties of situs or 'where' (such as being near or distant from a place) belong to it at all; rather, an angel is said to be 'in place' only insofar as it is in the located body according to its effect—as a mover is in what is moved, or as an immediate cause is in its effect. Proponents of this view hold that an angel's moving a body requires no spatial proximity of the angel to the place, nor any real exhibition of its presence to the located body at all, but only a proportion between the angel and the mobile body under the aspect of mover and mobile; given this proportion, the angel moves the body whenever it wills (being free in moving), and when it moves it is said to be 'in place' in the sense just described.
claims: Opinion 3: an angel is in place only in the sense that it is in its effect as mover is in the moved, requiring no spatial proximity or real presence, but only proportion between mover and mobile
concepts: presence as being in one's effect

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e895.summary: Rejects Opinion 3: given a proximate and sufficient cause of some action, unimpeded, the action must follow; yet we observe that even given the requisite proportion between active and passive, motive and mobile, with every impediment excluded, motion or action does not follow unless the active is really present to the passive; hence mere proportion between agent and patient is not a sufficient reason for acting or moving—real presence of one to the other is also required. This major premise is self-evident, and the minor (that mere proportion is insufficient without real presence) is even granted by the opinion's proponents in corporeal cases: they concede, and it is self-evident, that for one body to heat another, mere proportion of the heating and heatable is not enough—their approximation is also required, per Aristotle's text in De Generatione I. Yet these same proponents deny this requirement for non-quantified things (angels), without assigning any reason—they simply assert it. For even in bodies, approximation is required for acting only because it makes the active present to the passive, and remoteness impedes action only because the active is then absent from the passive; just as not everything acts on everything but a determinate agent on a determinate patient, so not everything acts in any manner but in a determinate manner—not while absent and to an absent thing, but while present and to a present thing—and this holds generally in every action and motion that presupposes a subject.
claims: Mere proportion between agent and patient is insufficient for action; real presence of one to the other is also required, as the corporeal case of heating shows
Opinion 3's proponents grant this requirement for bodies but deny it for angels without justification
The requirement that the agent be present (not merely proportioned) to the patient holds generally for every action and motion presupposing a subject
concepts: proportion versus real presence as conditions of causation
Aristotle De Generatione on approximation in heating
generality of the presence requirement for causation

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e947.summary: Anticipates a reply on behalf of Opinion 3: someone might say that in an angel's moving a body, presence of the angel to the body is indeed required, but not real presence as in corporeal cases—only presence 'according to reason,' since it seems to suffice for moving that the motive be present to the mobile under the aspect of mover to moved, i.e., as knower to known and willer to willed (a non-real presence), unlike bodies, which move other bodies through an inherent form and so require real proximity.
claims: A possible defense of Opinion 3: an angel's presence to what it moves need only be presence 'according to reason' (as knower to known, willer to willed), not real/physical presence, unlike bodies which act through an inherent form requiring real proximity
concepts: presence according to reason versus real presence
knower/known and willer/willed as models of non-real presence

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e980.summary: Rejects this defense: even granting the angel has a single power by which it understands, wills, and moves, that power functions differently under each aspect—as intellective it only directs toward motion, as volitive it only commands motion, as motive/executive it actually and immediately moves. Since a mediate and remote cause need not be simultaneous with its effect, but only an immediate and proximate cause must, the angel's understanding and willing do not require real presence of the body to be moved (being only a remote cause of the motion), but its actual moving does require real presence (being the proximate cause). Illustrated by an analogy: if heat itself were volitive and calefactive, willing would not require real approximation of the willed object, but heating would. Hence the major premise (that presence suffices without real proximity) must be understood of the immediate moving cause, under which sense the minor premise (that such presence is not real) is false.
claims: The angel's power functions as remote cause (intellect, will) and proximate cause (actual moving) differently; only the proximate cause requires real presence
Understanding and willing do not require real presence of the body to be moved, but actual moving does
Therefore Opinion 3's defense fails: real presence is required for the moving itself, even if not for the antecedent acts of intellect and will
concepts: real presence required only of the proximate/executive cause

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1013.summary: States Opinion 4: an angel's essence is nowhere, neither by reason of itself or anything existing in it, nor by reason of operation passing outward, such that definitive place or situs is owed to it—agreeing with Opinion 3 on this point. But it differs in holding that just as the angel is nowhere as to situs, so it is present to any body it can move by the presence of 'order,' not situs, whether or not it actually moves that body; when it does move a body, it is said to be there specially, by a kind of appropriation, because its power is manifested there, though its real presence to the place precedes its operation there. Proponents are moved by the principle (proved above) that motion and every action presupposing a subject requires the presence of mover to mobile and agent to patient prior to acting; but an angel can act on many bodies at once or successively, so before acting it must be present to any body simultaneously—for if it were first present to only one and then another, it would be hard to say why it was present to this one rather than that one (since, ex hypothesi, it has not yet acted on either), and the same difficulty would remain even if it had acted on one, since operation does not cause presence but presupposes it; moreover, if it were present to one and not another, it would seem to be defined by place, contrary to what this opinion holds, and it could not become present to another except through motion, and to say an angel is moved through its own essence is not intelligible. Hence this view holds the angel simultaneously present to every body it can move, prior to moving any of them, persuaded by the parallel that what situs does among bodies, order does among spirits (per Augustine): the heavenly body, having causality over all generable and corruptible things, is present to all of them by situs in such a way as to be able to act on all; likewise an angel, having causality over certain bodies as to local motion, is present to all of them by order, such that it can act on any when it wills (even if it does not always act, by reason of its freedom)—with the difference that the heavenly body's presence by situs to the totality of contained bodies is not immediate to each one individually but mediated through the continuous whole (nearer parts immediate, farther parts mediate through the nearer), whereas the angel's presence by order to any body it can move is not impeded by one body from being equally immediate to any other—illustrated by the rational soul, which, though not quantified, is wholly and immediately present in one part of the body (the head) without being thereby impeded from being immediately wholly present in a distant part (the foot); the same holds for the angel with respect to any body it can move, except that the angel, unlike the soul, is not the form and act of the body.
claims: Opinion 4: an angel's essence is nowhere as to situs, but it is simultaneously present, by 'order' rather than situs, to every body it can possibly move, prior to actually moving any of them
This presence-by-order is unimpeded and equally immediate to any of those bodies at once, unlike the heavenly body's mediated presence-by-situs to the corporeal totality

The analogy of the rational soul's whole and immediate presence to distant bodily parts (head and foot) without impediment illustrates how an angel can be equally immediately present to many bodies by order

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1138.summary: States the first of six doubts (dubia) raised against Opinion 4: if an angel is simultaneously present to every body it can move, it seems to follow that the angel is everywhere, just as God is—which seems improper.
claims: Doubt 1: Opinion 4 seems to entail that an angel is everywhere like God, which seems inappropriate

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1151.summary: States the second doubt: if an angel is simultaneously present to any body it can move, it seems it could simultaneously move all those bodies at once, since the reach of its power to act seems to extend as far as its essence's coexistence extends.
claims: Doubt 2: Opinion 4 seems to entail that an angel could simultaneously move all bodies to which it is simultaneously present

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1164.summary: States the third doubt: bodies movable by one angel are movable by any other angel equally; so by the same reasoning that grounds one angel's presence to those bodies, any other angel—and hence many or even all angels—would be simultaneously present there too, which is not held to be the case.
claims: Doubt 3: Opinion 4 seems to entail that many or all angels would be simultaneously present wherever one angel is, since the same movable bodies are movable by any angel

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1177.summary: States the fourth doubt: if God made another world, or several, without angels, would an already-existing angel be naturally present to every body of each such world, or not? If it would be present by the same reasoning, then were God to make infinitely many corporeal worlds, every angel would be present to all of them—which is not true unless each angel were infinite. But if it would not be present, it follows that the angel is definitively confined to this world, contrary to what Opinion 4 asserts.
claims: Doubt 4: Opinion 4 faces a dilemma from hypothetical additional or infinite worlds, seeming to entail either infinite angelic presence or definitive confinement to this world
concepts: dilemma of universal presence versus definitive confinement

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1199.summary: States the fifth doubt: Damascene (II.2) states expressly that angels, when in heaven, are not on earth, and when on earth, are not in heaven; hence an angel is not simultaneously present to every body.
claims: Doubt 5: Damascene's testimony that angels in heaven are not on earth (and vice versa) seems to contradict Opinion 4's claim of simultaneous presence to every movable body

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1212.summary: States the sixth doubt: a separated soul does not seem to have order to any body except its own (which no longer exists), neither as its form nor as a mover (since it is not held able to move other bodies), and it is hard to conceive another kind of order by which the soul could be present to any body; hence, at least, the separated soul would be nowhere—which seems erroneous.
claims: Doubt 6: Opinion 4's account of presence-by-order does not seem to apply to the separated soul, which would then be nowhere, an apparently erroneous conclusion
concepts: separated soul's lack of order to any body

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1231.summary: Reply to Doubt 1: either no angel can move all bodies locally, or if there is such an angel, it is still not everywhere as God is, since God is everywhere as the cause that fills every place with its effects, conserves every place and everything located, and whose first operation does not presuppose the entity of place or the located thing in order to act but produces the whole thing; an angel is everywhere in none of these ways, but only insofar as it has, from the order of nature, an aptitude to move any body, and on that basis is present to any body it can move, since without such presentiality it could not move it—and God and nature do not fail in what is necessary.
claims: Even an angel capable of moving all bodies would not be everywhere in God's sense, since God's ubiquity consists in filling and conserving every place as cause, not presupposing place's existence to act
An angel's presence to any movable body is grounded only in its natural aptitude to move it, required for the possibility of moving, not in causal universality like God's
concepts: distinction between divine and angelic modes of universal presence

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1260.summary: Reply to Doubt 2: little can be known of the extent of an angel's power to move bodies simultaneously—how many or how great; but it need not follow that an angel could simultaneously move all bodies to which it can be simultaneously present, just as a man need not be able to simultaneously move all bodies to which he is simultaneously present by bodily contact, even granting he could move each of them successively; the power to move need not be proportioned to match the extent of presence.
claims: It does not follow from an angel's simultaneous presence to many bodies that it can simultaneously move all of them
The extent of a power to move need not match the extent of presence, as the human case of bodily contact illustrates
concepts: non-proportionality of presence and active power

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1282.summary: Reply to Doubt 3: it is not improper for all, or at least some, angels to have a similar relation of presence to all bodies, such that 'all things are full of gods,' as was said [by an ancient authority]; this entails no confusion among angels, either as to their natures or as to situs, since their presence is not situal.
claims: Multiple or all angels sharing presence to the same bodies is unproblematic, since presence-by-order does not entail spatial confusion among distinct natures

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1298.summary: Reply to Doubt 4: if God made another corporeal world, or several, one could say that each angel would be present to any body of any such world by the presence of order, not situs. As for infinitely many worlds: according to some, God could not make an actual infinite, since this implies a contradiction; if that is true, the hypothesis should not even be entertained, since it would be not merely impossible but incompossible—that is, self-contradictory—and what is self-contradictory can in no way be posited, since its opposite always follows from positing it.
claims: An angel's presence-by-order would extend to any additional corporeal worlds God might make

The further hypothesis of infinitely many worlds is dismissed as incompossible (self-contradictory) on the view that an actual infinite cannot be made, and so should not be entertained as a real difficulty
concepts: presence by order extended to hypothetical worlds

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1329.summary: Reply to Doubt 5: Damascene's words should be understood not of the angel's presence to place absolutely (since the angel is in fact simultaneously in heaven and on earth in that sense), but of the presence manifested through operation; as already explained, it is not necessary that an angel be able to simultaneously move all bodies to which it is simultaneously present—rather, while it moves in one place it does not move in another, and is said to be in one place and not the other because its presence is manifested through operation here and not there.
claims: Damascene's statement concerns presence as manifested through operation, not absolute presence, resolving the apparent conflict with Opinion 4
concepts: manifested presence through operation versus absolute presence

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1351.summary: Reply to Doubt 6: as far as its own nature is concerned, the separated soul could be said to be nowhere; however, by divine appointment it is somewhere—namely in heaven, hell, or wherever God assigns it according to its merits or demerits. All of this is said without any assertion or personal commitment, only by way of inquiry, so as to give occasion for more skilled persons to investigate further.
claims: The separated soul is naturally nowhere but is somewhere by divine appointment, according to merit or demerit
The entire preceding discussion of opinions 2-4 and the doubts is offered inquisitively, without settled assertion
concepts: divine appointment of the soul's post-mortem location

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1372.summary: Reply to the first opening argument (d1e115): it belongs to an angel to be in place by reason of its essence—not circumscriptively (which does not even belong to material substance, as the objection itself argued) nor definitively in the sense that a determinate situs with spatial proximity and distance belongs to its essence, but according to the 'order' already discussed. It also belongs to an angel to be in place through operation, as to manifestation, and in this way nothing prevents it from sometimes being nowhere (in the manifested sense)—though some say an angel cannot ever fail to operate on place at all, on pain of the universe being disconnected unless spiritual things are bound to corporeal ones through operation (understanding 'operation' broadly as any contact or application of power to place). This further claim is called frivolous: since an angel freely operates on body, it can wholly refrain from operating without thereby disconnecting the universe, because the universe's connectedness requires only the natural degree and order of its parts, not the actual operation of every part; and if actual operation were required, it would suffice for the lowest angel alone to move a body while the others remain connected through other spiritual operations such as illuminations—in which case all angels but one would, by this logic, be nowhere through operation. It is further found strange to deny that such contact-operation is 'moving,' since every operation passing into external matter is directed either to form or to place, and an angel's action on a body can only reach form through local motion; nor can one conceive what contact an angel could have with a body apart from motion, except by imagining a corporeal angel that keeps its 'hand' on a mobile body without always moving it—which is ridiculous.
claims: An angel is in place by essence, in the sense of 'order' rather than circumscriptive or definitive-situal presence, and by operation as to manifestation

An angel can, at times, have no operation manifesting its presence anywhere, since its operation is free, and this does not disconnect the universe, whose connectedness requires only the natural order of parts, not universal actual operation
The claim that non-local 'contact' operation without motion is possible for angels is rejected as unintelligible except by absurdly imagining a corporeal angel
concepts: ordo as ground of essential presence

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1440.summary: Reply to the second opening argument (d1e157): Boethius speaks of being in place circumscriptively—this is the sense in which it is the common conception that incorporeal things are not in place, but not in any other sense.
claims: Boethius's dictum about incorporeal things not being in place concerns circumscriptive presence only, leaving other modes of presence untouched

jsnvu6-d1e1826-d1e1451.summary: Reply to the sed contra argument (d1e169), noting it is already answered by what has been said: angels are where they operate not only through the presence of their essence but through the manifestation of that presence.
claims: The sed contra (Damascene: incorporeal nature is where it operates) is affirmed and integrated: angels are where they operate both by essential presence (order) and by the manifestation of that presence through operation
concepts: reply integrating essential presence and manifested presence

jsnvu6-d1e1826.summary: Question 3 asks whether an angel is in place. Two objections deny it (place would have to follow essence, power, or operation, none of which seem to fit an incorporeal substance; and incorporeal things are commonly held not to be in place), while the sed contra, from Damascene, affirms that an incorporeal nature is where it operates. The responsio first fixes clear preliminaries: strict circumscriptive presence never applies to angels, and even the broader 'natural place' sense fails since angels have no natural inclination to one place over another. It then surveys and largely rejects four opinions. Opinion 1 (angel is definitively in place by reason of its finite essence, on three grounds: analogy to divine infinity, priority of essential presence to operation, and status as part of the universe) is refuted in detail: essential limitation, unlike quantitative limitation, entails no necessary relation to a proportioned place; the priority-to-operation argument is defused by showing immediate presence is broader than local proximity (illustrated by form's presence to matter); and the part-of-the-universe argument is refuted by distinguishing the corporeal universe from the universe of all things, so that spatial differentiae proper to corporeal parts need not extend to incorporeal ones. Opinion 2 (essence is in place via operation, but as the essence's own property) and Opinion 3 (angel is 'in place' only as mover is in its effect, without any real presence or proximity) are also rejected—the latter because action always requires real presence of agent to patient, not mere proportion, as even the corporeal case of heating shows. Opinion 4 is presented as the preferred view: an angel's essence is nowhere as to situs, but is simultaneously present, by 'order' rather than situs, to every body it can move, unimpeded by that presence's extension to other bodies (illustrated by the soul's undivided presence to distant bodily parts). Six doubts against this view are raised and answered, distinguishing angelic from divine universality of presence, denying that co-presence entails co-omnipotence or confusion among angels, dismissing an infinite-worlds difficulty as self-contradictory, reconciling Damascene's testimony by distinguishing absolute presence from operationally manifested presence, and allowing that the separated soul, naturally nowhere, is placed by divine appointment according to merit. The question closes by applying the 'order' account to answer both opening objections and the sed contra.
claims: An angel is not in place circumscriptively (like a body) nor definitively by reason of essential limitation, nor merely as a mover is in its remote effect without real presence

The angel's true mode of presence to place is by 'order,' a non-spatial, non-circumscribed presence distinct from both bodily situs and from mere causal proportion, which nonetheless requires real (not merely notional) presence prior to and independent of the angel's actual operation
An angel can be simultaneously present by order to every body it is capable of moving, without confusion among angels and without this constituting divine-style ubiquity
An angel's presence 'in' a particular place as commonly experienced is a matter of the manifestation of its presence through operation, not a change in its underlying order-presence
The separated soul, naturally nowhere, occupies a place only by divine assignment according to merit or demerit
concepts: ordo versus situs versus circumscriptive presence
real presence as a precondition of causal action
